title: Right Speech
speaker: Seiu Hannah Sullivan
summary: Seiu Hannah Sullivan takes up right speech, the final talk in the summer series on the Noble Eightfold Path, drawing on the Pali Canon's abstentions and the Buddha's five questions. Seiu recalls adolescent gossip and Seiu's brothers' satire, then describes a post office visit where harsh thoughts about a clerk gave way to talk of his sewing once he saw Seiu's rakusu. Seiu's dad's heated arguments end when Seiu suggests changing the conversation. Seiu reads Norman Fischer on language as dialogue and Thich Nhat Hanh on deep listening, then sends the group into small breakout rooms to share where right speech has been present or absent.

sentences.text: *An unsurpassed penetrating and perfect dharma is rarely met with even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
Hi, everybody.
Let me know if my voice gets too soft, you guys out there on the far reaches.
And hello to our Zoom contingent.
It is started.
Yeah.
Edie, Dave, Kate, Jeff, Karen.
Welcome.
Thanks, everybody, for coming out tonight.
It takes a little effort, so thank you.
I'm going to talk tonight about right speech, or sama Vaka, as it's called in Pali.
This is the final night of our summer series on the Noble Eightfold Path.
The talks have been recorded, and they're easily available on our website.
I'd like to thank Tim, who invited the practice leaders to speak, and everyone who prepared and gave talks.
They've all been really interesting.
Just to review, we have right view and right resolve.
These are the wisdom, or development of insight, pieces.
Right speech, right action and right livelihood are the ethics.
Right effort, right mindfulness and right concentration are concentration, or control of the mind.
These topics were so beautifully shared by Desiree and her shuso class in this winter's practice period.
We were invited to choose one element to focus on during the period.
Having just gotten into a little bit of hot water for sharing something I hadn't realized was not yet public information, I chose right speech.
And what is right speech?
The Pali Canon says: abstaining from lying, from divisive speech, from abuse of speech, and from idle chatter.
This is called right speech.
Hand in hand with right speech goes silence.
Shakyamuni Buddha was heard to say, "Do not speak unless it improves on silence."
The Buddha thus explains right speech in the Pali Canon as can be stated in the form of five questions.
Is it timely?
Is it time for me to say this, or is it time for someone to hear it?
Is it truthful?
Is it pleasant?
Is it beneficial?
Is it kind?

As Bob Rose mentioned last week, a group of us have been studying the precepts, and it just happened that our topics for this week's class were the interface of this topic, with precepts six and seven spelling out how we can work with the notion of right speech.
Primarily, as Bob reminded us, that's the three pure precepts: do good, avoid evil, and benefit all beings.
Keep that in mind anytime you open your mouth.
Specifically, those precepts are about not speaking ill of others, and not speaking of others in a way that puts us above them.
Really, it's only with humility that we can approach this material.
Humility is not an abundant quality in adolescence.
Much of my humor in childhood and youth was formed around satire, irony and, let's face it, making fun of others.
My three brothers were masters of it.
One brother sat on the bench on the basketball team and ran color commentary with the guy next to him, and I can imagine what he said about every single player.
This was a rich vein: hierarchy, putting the speaker on the top.
That's us, that's me, the speaker.
We all had a keen eye for anything outside the norm, anything outside a fairly narrow norm, meaning, for me, white middle-class America.

I was privileged to live in a community that was largely Jewish, so I had a little bit of diversity, and I managed to avoid, or at least partially escape, the white Anglo-Saxon Protestant mode that prevailed in the Midwest.
There was a distinct absence of poverty where I lived, so the expectation that people would be well-dressed, clean, educated and well-mannered was the prevalent expectation.
How one dressed, looked and presented was key to one's status and placement in the social order of the adolescent community.
And then there's gossip.
What school child escapes?
That body of whispered assessment comes from inclusion and exclusion.
You're either the victim, the perpetrator, or the chuckling audience, and it's a very comfortable ground of being when you're immersed in it.
It's really familiar, and it's kind of fun when you're in the group that's doing the talking.
But often I would have the thought: so what are they saying about me when I'm not here?
I have found a great help in a suggestion of not speaking of another who is not in the same room.
Not always easy, and I certainly don't always do it, but it's a nice watchword.
It's not possible all the time.
We have to choose who's on the team, who gets the job, and sometimes what to do about a disruptive member of a group for the sake of the greater good.
But idle chatter does not need to be included in an assessment of others.
In the twelve steps, it's called taking inventory.
I love this idea.
We're asked to make a fearless and searching moral inventory of ourselves as we work through the steps, which weave so well into our Buddhist ethic.
And in a little twist of the hallowed steps language, we are cautioned that to take another's inventory is just not a good idea, ever.
This fits with the study of the precepts, if I might again mention that study.
We always try to remember that the precepts are for ourselves.
When I'm studying the precepts, I'm studying the precepts for me, not for Thales, and I'm not going to talk about whether Desiree is living up to her precepts.
It's personal, and it ripples out to everybody.
I just don't have the right to assess or to take inventory on whether somebody else is breaking a precept or upholding a code of ethics.
Don't we have enough to think about with our own behavior?
I think some of us feel like we came into our spiritual practice in the adolescence of our spiritual brain.
So with what often feels like great pain and the effort of experience, we pass from adolescence to a more mature point of view.
Choosing what we talk about, the level of conversation, we can actually teach ourselves to develop how and what we talk about with one another.
A reference to another person can be [unclear: "clean, has trouble with interaction with others, is quite different from brain damage"].
Recently, my husband Jerry and I have become hooked on yet another foreign mystery series, this one featuring a woman named Astrid, who has Asperger's syndrome.
Of course, to make the series gripping, all kinds of liberties are taken, but the fascinating moments are when Astrid goes to her support group.
She goes to an autism support group, and part of their exploration is attempting to understand how neurotypicals behave.

I find it fascinating, and it has really helped me to understand that human behavior has a really wide range, rather than wanting anybody I might encounter to exist within a norm of what I have considered to be acceptable human behavior.
Kind speech is how it's often referred to when we talk about the Eightfold Path.
It's part of a process that begins in our mind.
We have to think the thoughts before we can speak them.
So we have the guideposts in the Noble Eightfold Path, and I asked Desiree in her hosanchiki, which one do you like best?
I believe you told me right view.

And I find that if I view the person I'm thinking about and wanting to be critical of as part of me, and me as part of them, I can't really get away with a judgmental view followed by judgmental speech without blaspheming myself, because I'm talking about all of us.
I may have a decades-old habit of seeing differences and judging them.
I may have a habit of seeing my view as best view.
This gets hard.
I have a knee-jerk reaction to someone waving a Confederate flag.
I live in a community known as Upriver in the Skagit Valley, which was populated, among others, by a group of people from North Carolina known as Tar Heels who came to log.
There's a special accent that goes with it, and a special sort of worldview that goes with it.
Whenever I hear that rural North Carolina accent, both original and adopted, I assume a belief system exists that I don't share, and I start to withdraw.
The other day I went to the post office to mail my rakusu off to Kathy, my teacher in California.
I didn't want it to get damaged in transit.
The Marble Mount post office is this iconic little tiny building that has an opening, and then there's a desk, and then there's kind of a back room.
It's really personal, and you never wait in line.
It's the easiest post office in the world to send things from.
Well, I had to wait for a while until the postal clerk could notice me.
There was no bell.
I was going "hi," and there's this guy sitting at the computer, and it took a long time for him to get up from his chair and then lumber into the customer area.
My thoughts were going a mile a minute.
Why is he taking so long?
He is so fat.
I don't like him.
Why does he have to be here?
He's wrecking my post office.
All of that got interrupted when I said I'd like to get some advice from you on how to mail this.
I pulled out my rakusu in its Ziploc baggy, and he just lit up.
He said, "Well, that is so nice.
Look at those tiny stitches, and they're so even, and all that handiwork.
You know, I do a lot of sewing.
I first started because I'm a hiker, and I couldn't find any gaiters to fit my legs because they're so big.
So I had to go out and find an industrial sewing machine, and then I made myself a pair of gaiters, and it was pretty fun.
Then I actually wound up making a whole lot of camping gear.
And yeah, this is really, really nice."
So I thought, well, since he's a sewer, I'll take it out and we'll look at it, and I wound up talking to him about it.
Then I asked him how to mail it, and he gave me perfect instructions with an envelope.
Go home, get some cardboard, just like Chris said.
Exactly.
He sent me home without paying for the envelope, and when I left, we both had a new friend.
But I had to go through a process of kind speech, right speech.
It had to follow a change of mind.
Most of us have done a lot of zooming over the past few years.
There's a nice tool that was initially offered, I think, by San Francisco Zen Center.
It might have been Berkeley Zen Center.
The concept is step forward and step back, and people were invited to consider what our normal reaction is when it's time to talk.
Are we somebody who always steps forward, always has their hand up for the first answer?
Or are we somebody who tends to just step back, and maybe not talk at all, and be in the background?
The invitation was change.
Try to be a step-forward person.
Try to be a step-back person.
Obviously this was for the sake of good group interaction, and I have to say I think it's been really effective.

It's a good thing to think about, because these habits are so deeply ingrained in us, and sometimes we need tools to work out of them, even if we say something different to ourselves, if we say a word every day that's different from our old habit-pattern response.
As I was preparing for this talk, I came across a website called Deep Dharma.
It's authored by two practitioners.
Andrew Cohen is especially focused on Nagarjuna, the Middle Way, Vasubandhu, some of the old writers and thinkers.
Carl Jerome was initially a student of Philip Whalen.
The two of them have a center called North Shore Meditation, and they have some lists.
I thought I might share some of their lists with you, because they're jogs for us.
This is six elements of right speech.
Only speak when conditions suggest you should speak, so that's: is it the right time?
Only speak truthfully.
We've found out in spades over the past few years that not everybody has the same truth, so you have to speak your truth.
Only speak when you have something to say that will be of benefit.
This extends not just to benefit for the person you're going to talk to, but benefit for everyone, for the greater body.
Always speak in ways that can be understood.
Don't use too much jargon.
Don't talk over somebody's head.
Only say it once.
If you said it truthfully, when conditions suggest that it's appropriate, and if it's beneficial, then saying it more than once is more argumentative than just talking.
I liked this one: never go on the battlefield.
Arguing is not right speech.
Being of benefit isn't about winning.
Now, some elements of wrong speech.
Number one, harsh, mean-spirited, threatening or angry words.
Falsehoods and slander is number two.
Slander is very much a part of our sixth precept study.
Gossip and small talk are third, and fourth is belittling others, and especially belittling others to raise your own status.
This is seventh precept all the way: not praising self at the expense of others.
Going on, there are some qualities, and one thing that I found very interesting was the idea of flattery.
It's one thing to compliment.
It's another to actually set out to flatter someone in order to get them to feel better about you, or to get an answer, get a response that you hope will be good.
Hinting: kids are really good at this.
When you want something, you kind of hint at it.

Being verbally passive-aggressive or bullying, using words to exert pressure in order to get something, and being on one's best verbal behavior in order to deceive another: that would be inauthentic speech.
So again, it was five ideas from the Buddha.
I will speak at the proper time, internally and externally.
I will state the truth as I know it.
I will speak gently from the heart, and one of the things that they talked about here was tone.
I know other women besides myself who become very reactive to our partner's tone, and when I've brought it up to my husband, he goes, "What are you talking about?"
But we were traveling with some friends a few years ago, and they call each other by their last name, which is Wickman.
Every once in a while we'd be traveling along and Kath's wife would say, "Wickman, tone."
That has become a little joke in my house.
I will speak for the others' good, beneficially for everyone, and I will speak from patience and compassion, not with enmity.

So up to now I have focused on being the first one to speak, but I think we get into a lot of trouble in conversation when we react and then reply before we've been able to utilize all these helpful suggestions.
Who here has not blurted out a caustic rejoinder to a loved one in the heat of the moment?
I learned this at home, as many of us did.
This is, to me, causality in action.
You say something, it hurts me, so I say something that hurts you, and then let the argument begin.
It took me years to get a handle on this.
When I said at home, I meant at my familial home.
My dad and I were always at each other.
It really took me many years to come to this life-changing moment when my dad was drilling down on some hot topic.
I suspect it was something about communism.

For once I didn't take the bait, and instead I took a breath and I said, "Dad, we have such limited time with each other, and we won't have forever to talk together, so let's change the nature of this conversation."
I don't know where that came from, but it worked, and my dad and I never had a fight again after that.
It really upped the quality of our relationship.
Of course, it required a good deal of noble silence on each of our parts, because you're just not going to agree all the time.
The whole Samish Zendo got a big laugh when Norman Fischer suggested one day that we get along so great at sesshin because we don't talk.
As soon as we start talking, that's when things start to get a little complicated.
In a slightly more formal way, Norman also said, or wrote, in his discussion of right speech:
*The Buddha similarly evidenced the subtle and nuanced understanding that words do not have fixed meanings and ought never to be taken at face value.
The meaning of words depends on context, who is speaking and listening, the tone of voice employed, the underlying attitude evidenced, and the situation in which the words are spoken.
The very fact that the Buddha did not recommend saying his exact words, he encouraged others to explain the teachings in their own words, didn't designate a special holy language,*
although we certainly love to use Pali as that perfect expression of the Buddha, but he didn't say it was.
*This all shows that he understood language to be a process, essentially a dialogue, a dynamic experience, rather than a tool of exact description or explanation.

Far from being a neutral conduit for the conveying of pre-existing meanings, the Buddha saw that language is an ever-shifting vehicle for the self, and that the way to clarify the self and the world is to hold language in an accurate and sensitive way.*
I'll finish with a quote from another one of our favorite teachers, Thich Nhat Hanh.
He said:
*Deep listening is at the foundation of right speech.
If we cannot listen mindfully, we cannot practice right speech.
No matter what we say, we cannot, sorry, no matter what we say, we will not be mindful, because we'll be speaking only our own ideas and not in response to the other person.
In the Lotus Sutra, we are advised to look and listen with the eyes of compassion.
Listening with your eyes of compassion, compassionate listening brings about healing.
When someone listens to us this way, we feel some relief right away.
A good therapist always practices deep compassionate listening.
We have to learn to do the same in order to heal the people we love and restore communication with them.*
So I thought we could go into small groups.
If you want to choose your small group by people who are sitting right near you, let's say groups of three to four.
And the prompt is: how has right speech been present or absent in my life, or anything else you'd like to say about it?
How much time?
Let's see, five, ten?
Yeah, four to five minutes.
I would love to thank you here.
Yeah, I think so.
If not, I can show you.
Okay, I'm going to try to put you guys in a breakout room.
So down here, it's not a touch screen, and you just want one.
Good.
And then I have to bring them back, right?
Yeah, yeah.
Close all rooms.
Okay.
And you know what?
I'm going to shut off record.
